motion: Are the miracles of Jesus unbelievable?

bridges.description: Whether testimony for Jesus’s miracles can make those extraordinary events believable.
The comparative evidential threshold imposed by violations of ordinary natural expectations.
Whether the transmission, memory, and authorship of the Gospel reports support historical confidence.
Whether analogous miracle traditions weaken a special inference to Christian miracle claims.
Whether resurrection and salvation claims belong to publicly checkable historical knowledge or faith commitment.
Whether the formal historical case makes Jesus’s miracles credible enough to believe.
Whether early witnesses had informed first-person access rather than merely sincere inherited belief.
Whether early sources, named Gospel transmission, and ordinary historical accuracy support the miracle reports.
Whether hostile and non-Christian testimony corroborates the claimed public reputation for miraculous acts.
Whether rival miracle traditions lack the early, close, costly, and multiply attested features claimed for Jesus.

sections.title: Probability, testimony, and the threshold for miracles
sections.rationale: The motion turns first on what evidence could make an extraordinary miracle report believable and how competing explanations should be compared.

sections.title: Historical sources, authorship, and memory
sections.rationale: Both sides directly contest whether ordinary accuracy, Gospel identity, eyewitness investigation, and memory support the miracle inferences.

sections.title: Witness sincerity, access, and martyrdom
sections.rationale: A central dispute is whether costly commitment supplies only sincerity or also informed access to the alleged events.

sections.title: Competing miracle traditions and hostile testimony
sections.rationale: Both sides test the Christian claims against other religious traditions and against purportedly hostile or independent testimony.

sections.title: Mythology, historical meaning, and closing epistemology
sections.rationale: The remaining dispute concerns mythic parallels and the closing distinction between historical evidence, experiential meaning, and faith commitment.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Across enough opportunities, highly improbable coincidences will occur without requiring a miracle.
moves.warrant: Shermer argues that when the full set of opportunities is counted, the law of large numbers predicts that unusual matches will sometimes occur.
moves.inference: Mere improbability does not establish divine intervention, so miracle claims require a stronger evidential standard.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the minimum complete passage stating the many-opportunities reasoning and its conclusion that highly unusual events will occur.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: given enough time the highly improbable will happen
moves.attributionRationale: The uninterrupted formal opening belongs to Shermer and follows his named handoff.
moves.importanceRationale: It establishes the baseline distinction between coincidence and divine miracle used throughout his case.

burdenContact.rationale: It defines why unusual occurrence alone cannot satisfy the evidential burden.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Belief should track the comparative probability of a miracle versus error in its testimony.
moves.warrant: After presenting Hume’s maxim, Shermer applies it to resurrection reports transmitted through alleged eyewitnesses and contrasts them with the accumulated experience of human mortality.
moves.inference: Misreporting, misperception, exaggeration, or transmission growth is more probable than a resurrection on the evidence offered.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span uses Shermer’s clear explanation and application after the garbled Hume quotation, ending with his transmission-error conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: a wise man proportions his belief to the evidence
moves.attributionRationale: This is Shermer’s uninterrupted formal opening explanation.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the main comparative rule by which he evaluates all later testimony.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly links extraordinary claims to comparative evidential weight.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Human memory changes through repeated recall and retelling rather than preserving a perfect recording.
moves.warrant: Shermer describes memories as continually edited and shaped by later recollections, family reports, and photographs.
moves.inference: Eyewitness-derived traditions can change even without deliberate deception.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact passage states the cognitive-memory premise and its mechanism without relying on any corrupted technical term.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: memories are constantly edited and changed
moves.attributionRationale: The passage is within Shermer’s uninterrupted opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It offers a nonfraud explanation for how sincere reports can become unreliable.

burdenContact.rationale: It challenges the reliability of later reports derived from memory.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: A contemporaneous non-Christian figure was described with a divine birth, miracles, disciples, persecution, ascent, and later written accounts.
moves.warrant: Shermer deliberately presents the biography as if it were Jesus before identifying it as Apollonius of Tyana.
moves.inference: Narrative resemblance alone cannot uniquely authenticate Jesus’s miracle tradition.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The contiguous passage contains the deliberately disguised comparison and its reveal, which the source notes require be preserved.
moves.attributionRationale: The comparison and reveal occur in Shermer’s formal opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It introduces the closest named comparator later answered by Vandeweghe.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that similar sacred biographies arise outside Christianity.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Divine-son, resurrection, redemption, and hero-journey themes recur across ancient traditions.
moves.warrant: Shermer points to early Christian comparison with sons of Jupiter, Dionysus and Osiris traditions, and the broader oppression-redemption hero pattern.
moves.inference: Christian miracle narratives can be understood within recurring mythic forms rather than as uniquely evidential.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage selects the connected Dionysus, Osiris, and hero-journey comparison through Shermer’s oppression-redemption conclusion, omitting earlier cumulative examples and garbled names from exact quotation.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: this is a very common hero journey
moves.attributionRationale: This is an uninterrupted portion of Shermer’s formal opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It provides the mythic-parallel argument answered in the con rebuttal.

burdenContact.rationale: It places Christian miracle motifs within a wider family of religious narratives.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: The Mormon founding story is presented as a recent miracle tradition supported by a signed group of claimed witnesses.
moves.warrant: Shermer describes Joseph Smith’s gold plates, the eleven-witness affidavit, revelatory translation, and the resulting sacred history.
moves.inference: Signed witnesses and a detailed religious origin story can arise in a tradition the audience nevertheless regards as implausible.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This complete contiguous comparator begins with Joseph Smith’s revelation, includes the eleven-witness affidavit and translation claim, and ends with Shermer’s explicit comparison to the Jesus story.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: eleven of his shall we call them disciples saw these gold plates
moves.attributionRationale: Shermer presents this comparator during his uninterrupted formal opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the actual Mormon witness argument directly answered by Vandeweghe.

burdenContact.rationale: It tests whether signed group testimony uniquely supports Christian miracles.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: A much later Marian miracle was reportedly witnessed by tens of thousands, yet the audience does not accept it.
moves.warrant: Shermer cites the reported solar event at Fatima and contrasts its large claimed witness count with Christian resurrection testimony.
moves.inference: Large witness counts do not by themselves make a miracle tradition credible to those outside it.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the complete Fatima comparison through Shermer’s challenge to the audience; the garbled place-name wording is not quoted or treated as error.
moves.attributionRationale: Shermer owns the uninterrupted opening passage.
moves.importanceRationale: It tests the audience’s evidential standard against a competing mass-witness claim.

burdenContact.rationale: It asks whether the same testimonial standard is applied across traditions.

moves.speaker: Luuk Vandeweghe
moves.claim: Early Christians endured Roman persecution without retracting their testimony.
moves.warrant: Vandeweghe invokes Tacitus’s description of Nero’s persecution and argues that people connected to the early apostolic testimony continued despite severe suffering.
moves.inference: Their costly persistence supports sincerity rather than conscious fabrication.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage begins with the Tacitus setting and ends with Vandeweghe’s explicit sincerity conclusion, without treating suffering alone as eyewitness access.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: they never went back on their testimony
moves.attributionRationale: This uninterrupted formal opening follows Vandeweghe’s named handoff.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the sincerity half of his stated sincerity-and-informedness case.

burdenContact.rationale: Costly persistence bears on whether testimony was knowingly invented.

moves.speaker: Luuk Vandeweghe
moves.claim: Peter both transmitted a miracle-filled account and was positioned to know whether public miracles occurred.
moves.warrant: Vandeweghe links Peter to Mark’s early preaching tradition, notes the unflattering portrayal of Peter, and describes Peter as part of Jesus’s inner circle who knew ordinary death and disability.
moves.inference: Peter’s testimony is presented as informed first-person commitment rather than distant inherited belief.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Vandeweghe’s explicit Peter-sincerity claim, links Mark’s miracle content to Peter, and then states Peter’s inner-circle access and ordinary knowledge of death as one complete chain.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Peter was part of the inner circle
moves.attributionRationale: The formal opening continuously belongs to Vandeweghe.
moves.importanceRationale: Peter is Vandeweghe’s principal example combining source transmission, direct access, and costly commitment.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly supports the claim that an early witness could assess the alleged events firsthand.

moves.speaker: Luuk Vandeweghe
moves.claim: Luke is presented as an investigator who interviewed people connected to Jesus and preserved named informants.
moves.warrant: Vandeweghe says Luke traveled with Paul, interviewed available witnesses, and repeatedly records miracle accounts with associated names.
moves.inference: The Gospel material is offered as investigated testimony rather than anonymous legend alone.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact passage states Luke’s investigative method and the claimed agreement of informants.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: he interviews everybody he can find
moves.attributionRationale: The passage is within Vandeweghe’s uninterrupted opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a core link in the claimed historical source chain.

burdenContact.rationale: It connects Luke’s narrative to purported witness investigation.

moves.speaker: Luuk Vandeweghe
moves.claim: Detailed accuracy in Luke’s voyage narrative is presented as evidence of careful historical practice.
moves.warrant: Vandeweghe cites accurate route, wind, island-location, and voyage-duration details before calling Luke meticulous and careful.
moves.inference: A generally careful historian deserves consideration when reporting the miracle-centered message of his associates.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span captures the strongest ordinary-accuracy examples and Vandeweghe’s explicit bridge to the miracle message; uncertain technical names are omitted from the semantic wording.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Luke is a first-rate historian meticulous thorough careful accurate
moves.attributionRationale: Vandeweghe is the sole speaker in this formal opening passage.
moves.importanceRationale: It supports source care, though the opponent later disputes the step from ordinary accuracy to miracles.

burdenContact.rationale: It uses ordinary historical precision to support the reliability of the source chain.

moves.speaker: Luuk Vandeweghe
moves.claim: James’s family relationship to Jesus and later martyrdom are presented as unusually informed costly belief.
moves.warrant: Vandeweghe identifies James as Jesus’s brother, formerly skeptical, later worshiping Jesus, and unwilling to deny him under threat of death.
moves.inference: A close family member was positioned to detect ordinary fraud or moral pretense and nevertheless committed at high cost.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains the complete James argument from non-Christian historical mention through family access and refusal to deny; its dramatic details are represented as the speaker’s claims.
moves.attributionRationale: The uninterrupted formal opening is Vandeweghe’s.
moves.importanceRationale: James is the second principal case combining intimate access, changed belief, and costly commitment.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that James possessed unusually close personal knowledge of Jesus.

moves.speaker: Luuk Vandeweghe
moves.claim: Hostile Jewish tradition is presented as conceding unusual supernatural activity while rejecting Jesus.
moves.warrant: Vandeweghe cites a Talmudic accusation of sorcery and argues that Jesus’s opponents and James agreed at least that Jesus performed extraordinary acts.
moves.inference: Agreement from opponents is offered as corroboration that miracle claims were not solely friendly invention.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span contains the Talmudic claim, Vandeweghe’s interpretation, and the explicit hostile-corroboration inference; garbled dates and names are not quoted.
moves.attributionRationale: Vandeweghe owns the uninterrupted formal opening passage.
moves.importanceRationale: It is his main hostile-testimony line and broadens the claimed evidential base.

burdenContact.rationale: It treats opponent testimony as corroboration of a public reputation for extraordinary acts.

moves.speaker: Luuk Vandeweghe
moves.claim: The Apollonius tradition is argued to rest on a single much later, interested, and fantastical source.
moves.warrant: Vandeweghe contrasts the claimed early Christian evidence with a source roughly a century and a half later, containing fantastical material and commissioned amid opposition to Christianity.
moves.inference: Apollonius is not an evidentially close parallel to Jesus even if the stories share motifs.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage begins with the named comparator and ends with the claim that it is a historical counterfeit; corrupted proper-name captions are not quoted.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the difference between Jesus and Apollonius is worlds apart
moves.attributionRationale: This is Vandeweghe’s uninterrupted formal opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers one of Shermer’s central named comparators.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the comparator lacks early and independent sourcing.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the analogy by contrasting the timing, number, motive, and content of the sources.

moves.speaker: Luuk Vandeweghe
moves.claim: Joseph Smith’s witnesses and conduct are presented as disanalogous to the early Christian witnesses.
moves.warrant: Vandeweghe says one witness described spiritual sight, early witnesses were excommunicated as liars, and Smith publicly denied conduct Vandeweghe says he practiced.
moves.inference: The Mormon comparator does not match the claimed informed and sincere Christian source chain.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains the complete rebuttal to the Mormon comparison and its conclusion that the Christian evidence should be taken seriously.
moves.attributionRationale: Vandeweghe is the uninterrupted speaker through the end of his opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It addresses Shermer’s modern religious comparator with a source-specific disanalogy.

burdenContact.rationale: It contests whether Mormon testimony shares the claimed Christian witness qualities.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the witness quality and source character of Shermer’s Mormon comparison.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: The Gospel names are later attributions to works whose authors were anonymous according to most biblical scholars.
moves.warrant: Shermer distinguishes the traditional names from the authors and gives a relative sequence from Mark through John.
moves.inference: The source chain cannot simply assume direct authorship by Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the complete authorship challenge at the beginning of Shermer’s formal rebuttal.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: these were names given to the books by the anonymous authors
moves.attributionRationale: The named handoff places this uninterrupted rebuttal with Shermer.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly attacks the named eyewitness source chain on which the con case depends.

burdenContact.rationale: It disputes the asserted identities linking texts to eyewitnesses.

responseComponents.description: Questions whether the Gospel author can simply be identified as the claimed investigator Luke.
Questions the direct link between Mark’s text and Peter.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: A narrative can be accurate in ordinary details while its extraordinary element remains unsupported.
moves.warrant: Shermer appends an explicitly invented alien abduction to a detailed and mostly accurate account of his trip, then notes that the audience rejects the abduction.
moves.inference: Corroborated background details and an additional witness do not supply extraordinary evidence for the extraordinary part.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The full hypothetical is necessary to preserve that it was invented and to reach the explicit claim-specific-evidence conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: of course I just made that up as an example
moves.attributionRationale: Shermer narrates and labels the hypothetical during his rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It is his clearest analogy for the gap between ordinary accuracy and miracle credibility.

burdenContact.rationale: It illustrates why evidence for ordinary narrative details does not meet the miracle threshold.

responseComponents.description: Uses an invented mixed true-false narrative to challenge the inference from ordinary accuracy to extraordinary truth.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: People across religious and political movements suffer and die for false beliefs.
moves.warrant: Shermer cites numerous non-Christian and secular movements whose adherents accepted suffering because they strongly believed a leader, cause, or ideology.
moves.inference: Costly death demonstrates conviction but is not evidence that the underlying miracle claim is true.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage begins with the suffering issue and ends with Shermer’s explicit conclusion that such suffering is not evidence.
moves.attributionRationale: Shermer is the uninterrupted speaker in the formal rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers the con case’s repeated appeal to martyrdom.

burdenContact.rationale: It restricts what costly sincerity can establish about truth.

responseComponents.description: Concedes that suffering can reflect conviction while denying that conviction establishes truth.
Challenges the move from Peter’s costly death to the truth of miracle claims.
Challenges the move from James’s costly death to the truth of miracle claims.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Islam also has a developed tradition of witnessed miracles attributed to Muhammad.
moves.warrant: Shermer lists miracle reports accepted by many Muslims with claimed eyewitnesses and supporting documents.
moves.inference: Popularity and claimed attestation do not distinguish Christianity from competing miracle traditions.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with the audience’s nonacceptance of Islam, then supplies the claimed attestations and miracle examples through Shermer’s structural comparison; corrupted individual wording is not quoted.
moves.attributionRationale: Shermer owns the uninterrupted rebuttal passage.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the broadest competing living-religion comparator in the formal speeches.

burdenContact.rationale: It tests whether Christian evidence is distinctive across religious traditions.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Knowledgeable Jewish interpreters reject Christian messianic miracle claims despite understanding the arguments.
moves.warrant: Shermer notes shared scriptures and informed rabbinic engagement while emphasizing a different expected messianic profile.
moves.inference: The evidence does not compel informed observers in the way publicly reliable knowledge normally would.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains the full disagreement argument and Shermer’s conclusion that religion depends on factors beyond ordinary evidence and reason.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: they know the arguments
moves.attributionRationale: The formal rebuttal remains Shermer’s through its closing thanks.
moves.importanceRationale: It broadens his objection from isolated testimony to persistent informed disagreement.

burdenContact.rationale: It questions whether the miracle conclusion functions as shared objective knowledge.

moves.speaker: Luuk Vandeweghe
moves.claim: The evidence for Jesus’s miracles is itself claimed to be extraordinary and weighty.
moves.warrant: Vandeweghe directly accepts the need to address extraordinary evidence and identifies his opening historical case as meeting it.
moves.inference: The evidential slogan does not decide the debate against miracles unless the offered historical evidence is first assessed.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span opens Vandeweghe’s rebuttal with his direct answer to Shermer’s evidential threshold; unrelated cosmological examples are retained only as part of his stated challenge and not expanded.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I do think that the evidence for Jesus miracles is extraordinary
moves.attributionRationale: The host handoff is excluded and Vandeweghe’s formal rebuttal begins clearly at event 1377.
moves.importanceRationale: It squarely joins the central evidential-threshold dispute.

burdenContact.rationale: It claims the formal case reaches the level needed to make the miracles believable.

responseComponents.description: Accepts that evidence must be weighty but asserts that the historical case supplies such evidence.

moves.speaker: Luuk Vandeweghe
moves.claim: The disciples’ costly commitment is distinguished from people dying for teachings received from others.
moves.warrant: Vandeweghe contrasts inherited ideological belief with adults who allegedly experienced repeated public miracles, supported by multiple witnesses and life change.
moves.inference: Examples of sincere but mistaken later believers do not answer the claimed combination of sincerity and firsthand access.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span preserves the explicit qualification between sincerity and first-person access through the stated evidential distinction.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: they died for something they experienced publicly as adults
moves.attributionRationale: This is Vandeweghe’s uninterrupted formal rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the key reply preventing martyrdom sincerity from being treated as the whole con argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It makes firsthand access, not suffering alone, the relevant distinguishing premise.

responseComponents.description: Agrees people die for false teachings but distinguishes alleged direct adult experience.
Contrasts the isolated invented story with repeated public and multiply witnessed events.

moves.speaker: Luuk Vandeweghe
moves.claim: Traditional Gospel identities are said to have uniform early external attestation.
moves.warrant: Vandeweghe cites agreement among early church fathers and uniform manuscript attribution from the beginning.
moves.inference: The named author traditions should not be dismissed as unsupported later labels.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This minimum complete passage states the external early-church and manuscript-attribution argument without the preceding garbled Greek internal illustration.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the manuscript evidence is uniform from the beginning
moves.attributionRationale: Vandeweghe is the sole speaker in this formal rebuttal passage.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly defends the source identities required by his eyewitness chain.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies internal and external reasons for accepting named Gospel transmission.

responseComponents.description: Answers anonymity with claimed internal author fit and uniform early attribution.

moves.speaker: Luuk Vandeweghe
moves.claim: Palestinian Jewish hostility to Hellenistic influence makes direct borrowing from pagan mythology historically unlikely.
moves.warrant: Vandeweghe points to the Hebrew Bible’s dominance in the New Testament and local resistance to pagan imagery and influence.
moves.inference: Shared motifs do not establish that Gospel miracle claims were copied from surrounding myths.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span states the borrowing challenge and the cultural evidence used to resist it.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: they strongly resisted hellenism and Hellenistic influences
moves.attributionRationale: The rebuttal passage is continuously Vandeweghe’s.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the historical mechanism objection to Shermer’s mythology comparison.

burdenContact.rationale: It denies the cultural transmission premise needed for a borrowing explanation.

responseComponents.description: Argues that motif similarity is insufficient without evidence of borrowing in a resistant Jewish setting.

moves.speaker: Luuk Vandeweghe
moves.claim: Recurring resurrection and redemption hopes can be interpreted as anticipations fulfilled in history rather than as disproof.
moves.warrant: Vandeweghe invokes C. S. Lewis’s distinction between mythic human hopes and the claim that one such pattern became historical in Jesus.
moves.inference: Mythic parallelism is compatible with, and on this view can support, Christian historicity.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains the complete alternative interpretation of parallels through the explicit conclusion that parallels do not necessarily undercut historicity.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: that story seems to have become history
moves.attributionRationale: Vandeweghe owns the uninterrupted formal rebuttal passage.
moves.importanceRationale: It answers the conceptual force of the myth-parallel argument after the historical borrowing reply.

burdenContact.rationale: It provides an alternative explanation for recurring motifs.

responseComponents.description: Reinterprets shared motifs as human hopes rather than evidence of fabrication.

moves.speaker: Luuk Vandeweghe
moves.claim: Normal memory errors do not plausibly explain wholesale invention of repeated life-changing miracles.
moves.warrant: Vandeweghe cites a study with reported 82% next-day and 81% three-month accuracy, concedes errors in details, and contrasts those with forgetting a central relationship or transformative event.
moves.inference: Memory fallibility permits peripheral error without erasing the central miracle testimony.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage covers the memory objection, the clear percentage comparison, acknowledged detail errors, and the central-event inference; the corrupted study count is not used.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: those are our best memories because they form who we are as people
moves.attributionRationale: This remains Vandeweghe’s uninterrupted formal rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers Shermer’s reconstructive-memory objection while conceding limited fallibility.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that source memory can preserve central events despite peripheral mistakes.

responseComponents.description: Concedes ordinary detail errors but denies that they explain forgetting transformative central events.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Objective factual claims differ from subjective preferences and private experiences in how they can be checked.
moves.warrant: In his formal closing Shermer contrasts countable public facts, tastes, altered-state experiences, and political value choices.
moves.inference: Miracle claims should be classified by whether they admit shared public verification rather than by their meaning to believers.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This complete closing framework begins with the truth question and runs through the distinction among factual, subjective, experiential, and political claims.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there are different kinds of knowledge statements or claims
moves.attributionRationale: The formal closing is clearly handed to Shermer after the excluded discussion.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the epistemic framework for his final application to Jesus.

burdenContact.rationale: It distinguishes publicly testable knowledge from subjective or experiential claims.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Jesus’s existence and crucifixion are ordinary historical claims, while resurrection and dying for sins require a different and much stronger basis.
moves.warrant: Shermer grants the probable historical person and crucifixion, contrasts resurrection with the accumulated experience that the dead do not return, and notes that informed non-Christians reject the evidence.
moves.inference: The resurrection is not established as objective, reliably checkable knowledge and is accepted within a faith tradition.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span applies Shermer’s closing epistemic framework to Jesus, resurrection, interreligious disagreement, and the distinction between faith and factual knowledge.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: you either believe it or you don't
moves.attributionRationale: This is Shermer’s uninterrupted formal closing.
moves.importanceRationale: It is his final motion-level synthesis of the historical and religious claim distinction.

burdenContact.rationale: It states why the central miracle remains unbelievable on the offered evidence.

responseComponents.description: Rejects the claim that the offered evidence elevates resurrection to objective historical knowledge.

moves.speaker: Luuk Vandeweghe
moves.claim: Jesus’s miracles are presented as historical evidence sufficient to support a serious commitment despite risk.
moves.warrant: Vandeweghe compares life to many open doors and argues that meaningful action requires commitment, then calls the miracle evidence early, extraordinary, and weighty.
moves.inference: The historical case makes belief and commitment reasonable even without eliminating personal risk.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the complete closing movement from indecision to commitment and the explicit description of the evidence; it does not depend on excluded discussion material.
moves.attributionRationale: Vandeweghe remains the sole closing speaker.
moves.importanceRationale: It connects the claimed historical evidence to the practical believability at issue in the motion.

burdenContact.rationale: It gives the final reason the miracles should be taken as credible enough for commitment.

selectionBalanceAudit.rationale: The evidential-threshold section has three pro moves and one con move because Shermer separately develops the many-opportunities baseline, comparative testimony rule, and claim-specific alien analogy, while Vandeweghe’s direct threshold reply is one integrated move. The witness section has two pro moves and four con moves because persecution, Peter, James, and the first-person/inherited-belief distinction are independently assessable con premises, while pro’s martyrdom counter and informed-disagreement line cover its distinct retained responses.

sections.rationale: No side requires a fourth row.
The con fourth row is required because investigation, ordinary accuracy, Gospel identity, and memory retention are four distinct source-reliability claims.
The con fourth row preserves the independently assessable distinction between inherited sincere belief and firsthand adult experience, separate from Peter, James, and general persecution.
The pro fourth row is required because Apollonius, Mormon witness testimony, Fatima mass witness testimony, and Islamic miracle tradition are distinct comparators that receive different answers.
No side requires a fourth row.
